Answer in combination with what you have learned: <image1> During a year, approximately how long is the time when sunrise at Jia is earlier than at Yi?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: The image shows a schematic map of island locations, with latitude and longitude lines labeled, and both Jia and Yi are located in the Southern Hemisphere. According to the relative positions on the map, Jia is southwest of Yi, that is, Jia is farther west than Yi and also farther south. From this it is judged: Jia is farther west, so according to the longitude factor it should have sunrise later than Yi; but Jia is farther south, and in summer in the Southern Hemisphere the daytime is longer, so sunrise would again be earlier than at Yi. The question stem states that on New Year's Day the sunrise times of the two places are synchronized, indicating that on New Year's Day, the effect of Jia's “being farther west causing later sunrise” and the effect of “being farther south causing longer daytime and earlier sunrise” exactly offset each other. If during a year Jia is to have sunrise earlier than Yi, then the longer-day advantage brought by Jia being farther south must be stronger than on New Year's Day, that is, the direct solar point is farther south than on New Year's Day, close to around the winter solstice on December 22. The movement of the direct solar point has approximate symmetry; after New Year's Day it has already deviated from the winter solstice by about ten days or so, so the corresponding other critical date is roughly near a similar number of days before the winter solstice. Therefore, Jia having sunrise earlier than Yi occurs only in the short period from around the winter solstice to around New Year's Day, on the order of about half a month.

ready3_open_rewrite.final_cot: The image shows a schematic map of island locations, with latitude and longitude lines labeled, and both Jia and Yi are located in the Southern Hemisphere. According to the relative positions on the map, Jia is southwest of Yi, that is, Jia is farther west than Yi and also farther south. From this it is judged: Jia is farther west, so according to the longitude factor it should have sunrise later than Yi; but Jia is farther south, and in summer in the Southern Hemisphere the daytime is longer, so sunrise would again be earlier than at Yi. The question stem states that on New Year's Day the sunrise times of the two places are synchronized, indicating that on New Year's Day, the effect of Jia's “being farther west causing later sunrise” and the effect of “being farther south causing longer daytime and earlier sunrise” exactly offset each other. If during a year Jia is to have sunrise earlier than Yi, then the longer-day advantage brought by Jia being farther south must be stronger than on New Year's Day, that is, the direct solar point is farther south than on New Year's Day, close to around the winter solstice on December 22. The movement of the direct solar point has approximate symmetry; after New Year's Day it has already deviated from the winter solstice by about ten days or so, so the corresponding other critical date is roughly near a similar number of days before the winter solstice. Therefore, Jia having sunrise earlier than Yi occurs only in the short period from around the winter solstice to around New Year's Day, on the order of about half a month.
